description: No ethics committee, IRB, or institutional approval is mentioned. The study or tool proceeds without documented ethics oversight.
example: A 5-month internet deployment is reported, but the paper never mentions IRB or ethics approval.

description: An ethics committee, IRB process, or institutional approval is explicitly mentioned or obtained.
example: The authors state the study was reviewed and approved by their institutional review board.

description: A specific ethics committee or review board is named or referenced.
example: Data handling was overseen by the university's named ethics review board.

description: No consent mechanism exists. Attackers or affected parties are not informed or given any form of consent.
example: Attackers interact with the decoy unknowingly; no notice or consent mechanism exists.

description: Attackers are treated as implicitly consenting adversaries with no active consent mechanism; assumes hostile intent.
example: A login banner states access is monitored and for authorized use only, implying notice to intruders.

description: Explicit informed consent is obtained from participants or parties interacting with the honeypot.
example: Participants sign an informed-consent form before interacting with the system.

description: Users or operators of the monitored network are not notified about honeypot deployment.
example: The honeypot is placed on the production network without notifying its legitimate operators.

description: The honeypot captures attacker usernames and/or passwords in plaintext or encoded form.
example: The honeypot records the usernames and passwords attackers submit during login attempts.

description: Full attacker sessions are recorded, including keystrokes, commands, screenshots, or terminal activity.
example: Every command and keystroke of each attacker session is logged for later analysis.

description: Malware binaries or exploit payloads are captured and stored by the honeypot.
example: Malware binaries dropped by attackers are collected and stored by the honeypot.

description: Full or partial network traffic (pcap) is captured from attacker interactions.
example: Full packet captures (pcap) of attacker traffic are recorded.

description: Attacker IP addresses are systematically logged and retained as identifiers.
example: The source IP of every incoming connection is logged and retained.

description: Data collected may constitute personal data under privacy regulations (e.g., email addresses, device identifiers, Bluetooth MACs).
example: Collected data includes email addresses and device identifiers that may count as personal data.

description: ICS/SCADA-specific protocol data (Modbus, S7comm, DNP3, BACnet, etc.) is captured from attacker interactions.
example: Modbus and S7comm protocol exchanges are captured from the emulated PLC.

description: Interaction data may include or reference medical identifiers (DICOM patient IDs, HL7/FHIR patient records).
example: The honeypot emulates a DICOM service and may capture patient-record identifiers.

description: Attacker behavioral patterns, command sequences, or interaction profiles are collected and analyzed.
example: Attacker command sequences and interaction patterns are profiled.

description: The authors discuss or not the ethical implications of collecting different types of data
example: For example, for one experiment a particular type of data might not be necessary and as such there is not justification on why it should be collected.

description: No data retention policy, deletion timeline, or archival strategy is documented.
example: No retention period, deletion schedule, or archival policy is stated for the collected logs.

description: A data retention policy or deletion schedule is explicitly mentioned.
example: Logs are automatically deleted after a stated retention period.

description: No discussion of data minimization, selective logging, or privacy filtering is present.
example: The system collects a rich set of data with no discussion of minimizing or filtering it.

description: Data minimization principles are explicitly applied or discussed.
example: Only fields needed for analysis are logged; a pre-recorded video stands in for a real camera feed.

description: Captured attack data or datasets are publicly released without restrictions.
example: The captured attack dataset is released publicly alongside the paper.

description: Captured data is shared in a controlled manner (e.g., requires application, institutional affiliation, or review). Share data on demand to other researchers but not necessarily to the public
example: The dataset is available only upon request and institutional affiliation.

description: Attack data is automatically or semi-automatically submitted to a third-party platform or service.
example: Captured samples are automatically submitted to VirusTotal.

description: The authors explicitely mention that they will not share the data for whatever reason
example: Neither the logs nor any dataset are released beyond the research team.

description: The honeypot deployment creates a risk of capturing or exposing personal or sensitive private data.
example: While capturing attacker IDs and IPs, the data collected could identify individuals.

description: The data collection practices may trigger GDPR or similar data protection regulation obligations, not discussed.
example: Attacker IP addresses are logged, which may trigger GDPR obligations the paper does not discuss.

description: Attacker IP addresses are collected without anonymization, raising privacy concerns under data protection law.
example: Attacker IPs are stored without anonymization or hashing.

description: The honeypot is deployed on or distributed to consumer-facing devices (e.g., mobile apps, Play Store), raising end-user privacy concerns.
example: The sensor ships as a consumer mobile app, raising end-user privacy concerns.

description: Data collected from or about non-attacker parties (victims, legitimate users, infrastructure operators) is captured without consent.
example: Data about legitimate users or operators is captured without their consent.

description: Data included in the honeypot deployment could be a privacy risk for the honeypot owner
example: For example, if a company deploys a database honeypot and the honeypot includes a fake database, they database could reveal private company information

description: No legal framework, jurisdiction analysis, or regulatory compliance is discussed.
example: No legal, jurisdictional, or regulatory analysis of the deployment is provided.

description: Legal jurisdiction, applicable laws, or regulatory compliance is explicitly addressed.
example: The authors note the deployment's jurisdiction and the privacy law that applies to the data.

description: The honeypot operates on regulated radio frequencies, raising spectrum regulatory compliance concerns not discussed.
example: The decoy transmits on regulated spectrum, a compliance issue left undiscussed.

description: Containment is achieved passively through logging only; the honeypot does not actively engage or respond to attacker infrastructure.
example: Documentation says the tool only logs and should not be actively exposed; containment is monitoring-only.

description: Active containment measures are implemented (e.g., containerization, network isolation, VM sandboxing, namespace isolation).
example: The honeypot runs in an isolated Docker/VLAN sandbox with egress filtering.

description: No containment or harm prevention measures are documented.
example: No isolation or harm-prevention measures are described.

description: A specific containment gap or risk is identified (e.g., proxy to real backend, malware escape risk, real device exposure).
example: The emulator proxies to a real PLC, a containment gap that could expose the live device.

description: The honeypot proxies to or connects with a real backend system, creating risk of real data exposure to attackers.
example: The front end forwards requests to a real backend system reachable by attackers.

description: A compromised or weaponized honeypot could be used to attack third parties; this risk is not addressed.
example: A compromised node could enable lateral movement to attack third parties; the risk is unaddressed.

description: Honeypot deployment in or near physical systems (ICS, medical devices, spacecraft, radio) creates risk of physical harm.
example: Because it emulates physical processes on a real PLC, a failure could affect physical equipment.

description: Deception is framed purely as an engineering or security mechanism with no ethical analysis or moral reasoning.
example: Deception is presented purely as an engineering technique, with no ethical reasoning.

description: The ethical dimensions of using deception against attackers are explicitly discussed or reasoned about.
example: The authors reason about whether deceiving attackers is ethically justified.

description: The honeypot actively transmits deceptive signals, responses, or content (beyond passive emulation).
example: The decoy actively sends fabricated responses rather than merely emulating a service.

description: Deception extends beyond cyber into the physical world (fake video feeds, simulated physical processes, radio signals).
example: Deception extends to a fabricated 360-degree video feed standing in for a real camera.

description: Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to generate dynamic, realistic deceptive responses to attackers.
example: A large language model generates realistic, dynamic replies to attacker commands.

description: No statements about researcher responsibility, ethical guidelines, or professional conduct are present.
example: The paper makes no statement about researcher responsibility or ethical conduct.

description: Researcher responsibility, ethical obligations, or professional guidelines are explicitly stated.
example: Responsibility is framed as defensive intent, with the authors committing to avoid harm.

description: Responsible disclosure of vulnerabilities, attacker identities, or threat intelligence is discussed.
example: Discovered vulnerabilities are handled through responsible disclosure.

description: The authors acknowledge the dual-use potential of the honeypot design or published findings.
example: The authors acknowledge the dual-use nature of publishing the design.

description: Attacker interaction data is transmitted to a third-party LLM API (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) for processing, without documented governance.
example: Attacker inputs are sent to a hosted LLM API with no stated data-governance controls.

description: AI-powered honeypot components operate without any documented AI-specific governance, bias assessment, or accountability framework.
example: The AI-driven honeypot operates with no AI-specific governance or accountability for its generated output.

description: The honeypot generates automated responses to attackers (scripted or AI-driven) without human review of each response.
example: The system auto-generates replies to attackers without human review of each one.

description: The honeypot is deployed on publicly accessible infrastructure facing real internet attackers.
example: Five instances were deployed on public IPs facing real internet attackers.

description: The honeypot is deployed in a controlled lab, testbed, or experimental environment rather than against live attacker traffic.
example: Evaluation ran in a closed lab testbed rather than against live traffic.

description: The honeypot operates in a simulated environment with no real-world attacker exposure.
example: The system is exercised entirely in a virtual testbed with no real-world exposure.

description: The honeypot is deployed in or adjacent to critical infrastructure (power grid, water treatment, transportation, telecommunications, space).
example: The decoy sits adjacent to a power-grid control network.

description: The honeypot or sensor is distributed directly to general consumers (e.g., via app stores, public downloads).
example: The sensor is distributed to the public through an app store (e.g., Play Store).

description: The honeypot is deployed on mobile devices carried into real-world environments.
example: The honeypot runs on mobile devices carried into real environments.

description: Deployed in an Industrial Control System context and explicitly discusses ICS-specific ethical concerns (safety, physical consequences, critical-infrastructure or cascading-failure risk).
example: Being an ICS honeypot, the paper explicitly weighs physical-safety and critical-infrastructure consequences.

description: Deployed in an Industrial Control System context, where physical consequences raise distinct ethical stakes, but the source does not explicitly address ICS-specific ethics; any ethics is implicit (e.g., via containment or safety isolation).
example: An ICS/PLC honeypot captures industrial commands without IRB oversight or any ICS-specific ethical discussion.

description: Deployed against IoT or embedded devices and explicitly discusses IoT-specific ethical concerns (scale
example: An IoT camera honeypot explicitly discusses device-owner privacy and scale-related harms.

description: Deployed against IoT or embedded devices but does not explicitly address IoT-specific ethical concerns; any ethics is implicit.
example: An IoT honeypot logs attacker data with no data governance or IoT-specific ethical discussion.

description: Deployed in a space or satellite context and explicitly discusses domain-specific ethical concerns (harm to space assets
example: The satellite honeypot reasons explicitly about avoiding harm to space assets (e.g., HoneySat).

description: Deployed in a space or satellite context but does not explicitly address domain-specific ethics; any ethics is implicit.
example: A satellite/space honeypot deploys with no explicit domain-specific ethical discussion.

description: Involves healthcare data or medical infrastructure and explicitly discusses domain-specific ethics (patient privacy, HIPAA, patient safety).
example: A medical-device honeypot explicitly addresses patient privacy and HIPAA obligations.

description: Involves healthcare data or medical infrastructure but does not explicitly address domain-specific ethics; any ethics is implicit.
example: A healthcare-adjacent honeypot handles patient-adjacent data with no domain-specific ethics discussion.

description: Honeypot deployed as or emulating a web application / HTTP service, raising web-application-specific ethical considerations (e.g., cloning real sites, handling submitted web form or credential data).
example: A honeypot mimicking a vulnerable web app or CMS login that logs attacker web requests.

description: Honeypot deployed on or emulating a mobile application / mobile device, raising mobile-specific ethical considerations (e.g., device-owner data, app-store distribution, carrying the sensor into real-world environments).
example: A low-interaction honeypot app running on phones carried into real networks (e.g., HosTaGe).
